whyWrongByChoice.D: rev is not one of the three genes described as encoding HIV structural proteins; p24 comes from gag.
whyWrongByChoice.E: tat is not one of the three genes described as encoding HIV structural proteins; p24 comes from gag.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with HIV has had an undetectable plasma viral load on antiretroviral therapy for several years. Researchers studying tissue from patients like him identify infected cells that express CD4 with the CCR5 coreceptor and that resist infection-associated apoptosis and cytotoxic T cell killing. Which cell type is most likely serving as this viral reservoir?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CD4+ helper T lymphocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Circulating neutrophils

choices.label: D
choices.text: Macrophages

choices.label: E
choices.text: Natural killer cells

explanation.summary: Macrophages and dendritic cells are less susceptible to infection-associated death and may serve as HIV reservoirs.
explanation.whyCorrect: HIV infects cells expressing CD4 plus at least one coreceptor (CCR5 or CXCR4): CD4+ T cells, macrophages, and dendritic cells. Infected CD4+ helper T cells are susceptible to apoptosis and immune-mediated killing, whereas macrophages and dendritic cells are less susceptible to infection-associated death and may act as reservoirs of the virus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Infected CD4+ helper T cells are particularly susceptible to apoptosis and cytotoxic T cell killing, the opposite of the described resistance.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD8+ cytotoxic T cells are effectors that kill infected cells; they are not described as HIV targets.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neutrophils are not listed among the CD4-bearing cells HIV infects.
whyWrongByChoice.E: NK cells contribute to CD4+ T cell destruction through antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity; they are not the reservoir.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman was diagnosed with HIV 4 years ago and declined treatment. She has been asymptomatic since a brief febrile illness at the time of infection, and her CD4+ T cell count has been stable at 600-650/uL. Which of the following best describes HIV activity in her body at this time?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Active replication, mainly in lymphoid tissue, at a set-point

choices.label: B
choices.text: Exponentially rising viremia outpacing the immune response

choices.label: C
choices.text: Replication confined to CNS cells behind the blood-brain barrier

choices.label: D
choices.text: Virus cleared from tissues by neutralizing anti-HIV IgG

choices.label: E
choices.text: Virus dormant as provirus with no ongoing replication

explanation.summary: Clinical latency is not viral latency: in the chronic phase HIV actively replicates, mainly in lymphoid tissue, at a steady set-point viral load.
explanation.whyCorrect: During the chronic phase patients are clinically latent and asymptomatic, but the virus is not latent. HIV actively replicates in the host, primarily in lymphoid tissues, and the viral load typically settles at a baseline set-point that stays steady for years.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The virus outcompeting the immune response describes the crisis (AIDS) phase, not a stable CD4 count years into infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Replication in the chronic phase occurs primarily in lymphoid tissues, not only in the CNS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anti-HIV IgG neutralizes and opsonizes free virions but does not clear the infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This confuses clinical latency with viral latency; the virus keeps replicating during the chronic phase.

questions.stem: Two 30-year-old men acquired HIV at about the same time and are both asymptomatic and untreated, with similar CD4+ T cell counts. Their physician wants the laboratory value that measures the replicative rate of each man's infection and whose baseline level best predicts how quickly each will progress. Which measurement should be followed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absolute CD4+ T cell count

choices.label: B
choices.text: Absolute CD8+ T cell count

choices.label: C
choices.text: Anti-HIV IgM antibody titer

choices.label: D
choices.text: Qualitative p24 antigen result

choices.label: E
choices.text: Set-point plasma viral load

explanation.summary: Viral load measures replicative rate, and a higher baseline (set-point) viral load predicts faster progression.
explanation.whyCorrect: Viral load should be monitored because it measures the replicative rate of the infection and its potential to destroy the cellular immune system. The baseline (set-point) viral load is a strong predictor of disease progression: a higher baseline correlates with faster progression.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD4+ count gauges the current extent of immune compromise, opportunistic-infection risk, and prophylaxis needs; it does not measure viral replication.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD8+ counts are not used to measure viral replication or predict progression.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IgM against HIV is part of the screening immunoassay, not a monitoring measure of replication or prognosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: p24 antigen detection is part of the initial screen for diagnosis, not a quantitative prognostic marker.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man with untreated HIV comes for follow-up. He feels well and has no history of opportunistic infections or malignancy. His CD4+ T cell count is 180/uL. Which of the following best classifies his infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute phase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Clinical latency

choices.label: C
choices.text: HIV Stage 1

choices.label: D
choices.text: HIV Stage 2

choices.label: E
choices.text: HIV Stage 3

explanation.summary: A CD4+ count below 200/uL is HIV Stage 3, also known as AIDS, even without an AIDS-defining illness.
explanation.whyCorrect: HIV is staged by CD4+ T cell count: Stage 1 is 500 or more cells/uL, Stage 2 is 200-499, and Stage 3 (AIDS) is below 200. In people aged 6 years or older, a CD4 count under 200/uL alone meets the definition of AIDS.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The acute phase is the first 0-12 weeks after infection, often with a normal CD4 count.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Feeling well does not override the CD4 criterion; a count under 200/uL defines AIDS.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Stage 1 requires a CD4+ count of at least 500/uL.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Stage 2 covers CD4+ counts of 200-499/uL; his count is below 200.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman undergoes routine HIV screening at an annual visit. Her HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody immunoassay is reactive. She is asymptomatic. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to establish the diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Begin ART now without any confirmatory testing

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD4+ T cell count to confirm the infection is present

choices.label: C
choices.text: HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody-differentiation immunoassay

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rapid IgG-only antibody test as an independent recheck

choices.label: E
choices.text: Repeat the same antigen/antibody immunoassay in 6 months

explanation.summary: A reactive antigen/antibody screen is confirmed with an antibody-differentiation immunoassay or NAAT.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the standard HIV testing algorithm, the first test is an HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody immunoassay detecting p24 antigen plus HIV-specific IgM and IgG. If it is positive, an antibody-differentiation immunoassay or NAAT confirms the diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Treatment decisions follow a confirmed diagnosis; the algorithm requires confirmation first.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD4 count gauges immune compromise but does not confirm HIV infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An IgG-only antibody test is not the confirmatory step in the algorithm.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Waiting 6 months delays diagnosis; a reactive screen should go straight to confirmatory testing.

questions.stem: A term male infant is seen at 16 days of life. His mother has HIV and was on antiretroviral therapy during pregnancy. The pediatrician wants to determine whether the infant is infected. Which of the following is the most appropriate test?

choices.label: A
choices.text: HIV nucleic acid test (NAT)

choices.label: B
choices.text: HIV-1/2 antibody-differentiation immunoassay

choices.label: C
choices.text: HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody immunoassay

choices.label: D
choices.text: Infant CD4+ T cell count

choices.label: E
choices.text: Maternal viral load at delivery

explanation.summary: Infants born to people with HIV are tested by NAT (at 14-21 days, 1-2 months, and 4-6 months), not by antibody-based screens.
explanation.whyCorrect: Maternal IgG crosses the placenta and causes false-positive antigen/antibody screens in the newborn, so the standard algorithm is not used. All babies born to people with HIV should be tested with NAT at 14 to 21 days of life, at 1 to 2 months, and again at 4 to 6 months.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibody-based differentiation also detects maternal IgG and cannot establish infant infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Transplacental maternal IgG can make this screen falsely positive in the newborn.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CD4 count does not diagnose HIV infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Maternal viral load informs transmission risk but does not diagnose infection in the infant.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman presents with 4 days of fever, pharyngitis, diffuse rash, and cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy. Three weeks ago a condom broke during intercourse with a partner who has HIV and does not take treatment. An HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody immunoassay is nonreactive. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Order a CD4+ T cell count to guide staging

choices.label: B
choices.text: Order a nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Order an antibody-differentiation immunoassay

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reassure her that HIV infection has been ruled out

choices.label: E
choices.text: Repeat only the immunoassay in 3 months

explanation.summary: A negative initial screen does not rule out HIV in a patient with acute retroviral syndrome and recent high-risk exposure; test by NAAT.
explanation.whyCorrect: One exception to the standard algorithm: if a patient has symptoms of acute retroviral syndrome and a recent high-risk exposure but a negative initial screen, HIV should not be ruled out. Instead, test by NAAT, which detects viral nucleic acid during the high-viremia acute phase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD4 count does not diagnose infection and may remain normal in the acute phase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The differentiation assay confirms a reactive screen; it is not the next step after a negative screen with high suspicion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HIV must not be ruled out on a negative screen when acute retroviral syndrome follows a high-risk exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Waiting months delays diagnosis of a symptomatic acute infection that NAAT can detect now.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man is newly diagnosed with HIV and has no evidence of drug resistance. He is ready to start treatment. Which of the following describes a common initial antiretroviral regimen?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A fusion inhibitor combined with one NNRTI

choices.label: B
choices.text: A single NRTI given as monotherapy

choices.label: C
choices.text: An INSTI combined with two NRTIs

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ritonavir combined with cobicistat alone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two protease inhibitors without any booster

explanation.summary: Common initial ART regimens pair an integrase strand transfer inhibitor with two NRTIs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because HIV mutates rapidly, treatment combines drugs from more than one class. Common initial regimens use an INSTI plus two NRTIs, such as bictegravir/tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine or dolutegravir plus tenofovir with emtricitabine or lamivudine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fusion inhibitors such as enfuvirtide are not routine first-line ART.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Monotherapy invites resistance in a rapidly mutating virus; ART combines drug classes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ritonavir and cobicistat are pharmacokinetic boosters that inhibit CYP450, not a stand-alone regimen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Two protease inhibitors from a single class are not the described initial regimen.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old nurse sustains a deep needlestick injury while drawing blood from a patient with HIV who has a detectable viral load. She presents to occupational health 20 hours later. Her baseline HIV test is sent. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Start daily oral PrEP and continue indefinitely

choices.label: B
choices.text: Start post-exposure prophylaxis now for 28 days

choices.label: C
choices.text: Start post-exposure prophylaxis now for 7 days

choices.label: D
choices.text: Start post-exposure prophylaxis only if fever develops

choices.label: E
choices.text: Wait for her baseline result, then decide in 1 week

explanation.summary: PEP is started as soon as possible (ideally within 24 h, no later than 72 h) and taken for 28 days.
explanation.whyCorrect: Post-exposure prophylaxis is antiretroviral medication given after a possible exposure such as a needlestick injury. It should be started as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours and no later than 72 hours, and is taken for 28 days, for example bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PrEP is taken before possible exposure by a person without HIV; this is a post-exposure situation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The PEP course is 28 days, not 7.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PEP is started promptly after exposure, not held until symptoms appear.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Waiting a week would pass the 72-hour window for starting PEP.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with HIV arrives in labor with an unknown current viral load. She receives an intravenous antiretroviral during delivery, and her newborn is started on the same drug orally as prophylaxis. Which adverse effect of this drug most requires monitoring in the infant?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anemia and neutropenia on the complete blood count

choices.label: B
choices.text: Flare of hepatitis B virus when the drug is stopped

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hyperlipidemia and insulin resistance on metabolic labs

choices.label: D
choices.text: Painful erythematous nodules at injection sites

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced renal function and low bone mineral density

explanation.summary: Zidovudine, used intrapartum IV and for neonatal prophylaxis, causes bone marrow suppression requiring CBC monitoring.
explanation.whyCorrect: Zidovudine is the classic drug for preventing perinatal transmission: IV zidovudine may be given intrapartum when maternal viral load is high or unknown, and it is commonly used for neonatal prophylaxis. Its key adverse effect is bone marrow suppression (decreased hematocrit, leukopenia/neutropenia, sometimes thrombocytopenia), so CBC monitoring is needed.

whyWrongByChoice.B: HBV flare on discontinuation is the classic warning for lamivudine in HIV/HBV coinfection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyperlipidemia and insulin resistance are protease inhibitor adverse effects.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Injection-site reactions characterize subcutaneous enfuvirtide.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Effects on kidney function and bone density are associated with tenofovir.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of vulvar pain and itching for 5 days. She also reports a thin vaginal discharge. Her temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F). Pelvic examination shows grouped, fluid-filled vesicles and several shallow, exquisitely tender ulcers on the labia majora. She has never had similar lesions. Which of the following is the most likely causative agent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Herpes simplex virus type 2

choices.label: B
choices.text: Human papillomavirus type 1

choices.label: C
choices.text: Human papillomavirus type 16

choices.label: D
choices.text: Human papillomavirus type 6

choices.label: E
choices.text: Varicella zoster virus

explanation.summary: Painful vesicles progressing to multiple shallow, tender genital ulcers are classic genital herpes, most often caused by HSV-2.
explanation.whyCorrect: The classic HSV presentation is a vesicular rash that progresses to multiple shallow, tender ulcers. HSV-2 causes the majority of genital herpes, and a primary episode is often more severe than recurrences, with pain, itching, discharge, and systemic symptoms such as fever.

whyWrongByChoice.B: HPV-1 causes cutaneous warts such as common and plantar warts, not painful genital vesicles.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HPV-16 is a high-risk oncogenic type that causes nonproductive, transforming infection, not vesicular ulcers.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HPV-6 causes anogenital warts, which are painless verrucous lesions rather than tender vesicles and ulcers.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Varicella zoster virus causes chickenpox; it is not the sexually transmitted cause of painful genital ulcers.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man has had four episodes of painful vesicles on the shaft of his penis over the past year. Each episode heals within 2 weeks and recurs at the same location. NAAT of a lesion swab during one episode detected HSV-2. Between episodes, the virus most likely persists in which of the following locations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anterior horn cells of the spinal cord

choices.label: B
choices.text: Basal cells of penile epithelium

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inguinal lymph node macrophages

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sacral dorsal root ganglia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trigeminal ganglia

explanation.summary: HSV-2 classically establishes latency in the sacral dorsal root ganglia.
explanation.whyCorrect: HSV infects sensory neurons and migrates to sensory ganglia, where the genome persists without producing virions. HSV-2 classically becomes latent in the sacral dorsal root ganglia; on reactivation, virions travel distally down the neuron to recreate ulcers at the original site.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HSV is latent in sensory ganglia; anterior horn cells are motor neurons.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Latency in basal epithelial cells is a feature of HPV, not herpes simplex virus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HSV establishes latency in sensory neurons, not in lymphoid macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The trigeminal ganglia are the classic latency site of HSV-1, not HSV-2.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman undergoes cervical biopsy that shows high-grade dysplasia. Molecular testing detects HPV-16 DNA integrated into the host genome of the dysplastic cells. These cells continue to accumulate DNA mutations without undergoing apoptosis. Which of the following viral protein actions most directly accounts for the survival of these damaged cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: E6 binding and inactivating Rb

choices.label: B
choices.text: E6 promoting ubiquitination of p53

choices.label: C
choices.text: E6 stabilizing Rb in its active form

choices.label: D
choices.text: E7 binding and inactivating Rb

choices.label: E
choices.text: E7 promoting ubiquitination of p53

explanation.summary: High-risk HPV E6 binds p53 and promotes its ubiquitination and degradation, so mutated cells escape apoptosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: High-risk strains such as HPV-16 and HPV-18 drive production of oncoproteins E6 and E7. E6 binds p53 and promotes its ubiquitination and degradation, allowing mutations to accumulate without apoptosis. E7 separately inactivates Rb, producing uncontrolled proliferation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: E6 acts on p53, not Rb.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neither oncoprotein activates Rb; E7 inactivates it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: E7 inactivation of Rb drives uncontrolled proliferation; loss of apoptosis is due to E6 degrading p53.
whyWrongByChoice.E: E7 targets Rb; it is E6 that promotes ubiquitination and degradation of p53.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man comes to the clinic because of a painful cluster of vesicles at the corner of his mouth that appeared 1 day ago. He has never had similar lesions. The physician wants to confirm the diagnosis and determine which viral type is responsible. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial test?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Microscopy of lesion scrapings for koilocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nucleic acid amplification of a lesion swab

choices.label: C
choices.text: Type-specific antibody serology of serum

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tzanck smear of an unroofed vesicle

choices.label: E
choices.text: Viral culture of vesicle fluid for 5 days

explanation.summary: NAAT of a lesion swab is the preferred initial test for oral or genital herpes and distinguishes HSV-1 from HSV-2.
explanation.whyCorrect: Detection of viral DNA by NAAT in swabs or scrapings from lesions is the preferred initial test. It is highly sensitive, especially early before healing begins, and specific, including the ability to distinguish HSV-1 from HSV-2.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Koilocytes are the cytopathic effect of HPV, not herpes simplex virus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Type-specific serology detects past infection and is used for high-risk asymptomatic people, not to diagnose an active lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The Tzanck smear is outdated; its cytopathic findings also occur with varicella zoster virus and it cannot type the virus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Viral culture is rarely used because it is slow, taking about 5 days to grow.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with a first episode of genital herpes confirmed by NAAT is prescribed valacyclovir. She asks whether the medication will rid her body of the virus. Which of the following best describes the effect of this treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blocks viral entry into sensory nerve endings

choices.label: B
choices.text: Eliminates latent virus from the sacral ganglia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prevents all recurrences after a single course

choices.label: D
choices.text: Shortens the outbreak but leaves latent virus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Silences viral episomes inside infected neurons

explanation.summary: Guanosine analogs such as valacyclovir reduce the severity and duration of HSV episodes but do not eliminate latency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Guanosine analogs inhibit viral DNA replication in actively infected cells, reducing the severity and duration of symptomatic infection. They do not eliminate the latent genome in sensory ganglia, so recurrences at the original site remain possible, and the patient can spread the virus during them.

whyWrongByChoice.A: These drugs inhibit viral DNA replication rather than viral entry.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antivirals do not eliminate latency; HSV persists in the ganglia for life.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Treatment of the initial episode does not prevent recurrences at the original infection site.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Guanosine analogs act on viral DNA replication; they do not silence latent episomes.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man comes to the clinic because of several painless, flesh-colored verrucous papules on the shaft of his penis. The lesions are diagnosed on examination, and he is prescribed topical imiquimod cream. Which of the following best describes how this drug eliminates the lesions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Arrests division of infected cells in metaphase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Denatures proteins within the wart tissue

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibits viral DNA replication as a nucleoside analog

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neutralizes virions with antibodies to capsid protein

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stimulates immune cells to kill infected cells

explanation.summary: Imiquimod is an immune response modifier that stimulates immune cells to kill HPV-infected cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Topical treatments for genital warts include caustic agents, cytotoxic agents, and immune response modifiers. Immune response modifiers such as imiquimod and interferon alpha act like part of the body's immune cells, stimulating other immune cells to kill virus-infected cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Metaphase arrest is the mechanism of cytotoxic agents such as podofilox and podophyllin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Protein denaturation is the mechanism of caustic agents such as trichloroacetic acid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Guanosine analogs such as acyclovir inhibit HSV DNA replication; they are not wart therapies.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antibodies to the major capsid protein are induced by HPV vaccination, not by imiquimod.

questions.stem: At a well-child visit, the parent of an 11-year-old girl asks how the routinely recommended vaccine against the pathogen that causes genital warts and cervical cancer is made. Which of the following best describes this vaccine?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Formalin-inactivated whole virions of HPV-6 and HPV-11

choices.label: B
choices.text: Live attenuated strains of HPV-16 and HPV-18

choices.label: C
choices.text: Messenger RNA encoding viral envelope glycoproteins

choices.label: D
choices.text: Purified E6 and E7 oncoproteins as toxoid antigens

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recombinant virus-like particles of major capsid protein

explanation.summary: The HPV vaccine (Gardasil 9) is a recombinant vaccine of major capsid protein that assembles into virus-like particles.
explanation.whyCorrect: The HPV vaccine is made from the recombinant major capsid protein of the virus, which self-assembles into virus-like particles. It includes types 6, 11, 16, and 18, reduces HPV infection by up to 90%, and is recommended for all children aged 9-12 years.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The vaccine is not made of inactivated whole virions.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The vaccine is a recombinant subunit product, not a live attenuated virus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HPV is a non-enveloped virus, and the vaccine is built from capsid protein, not envelope glycoproteins.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The vaccine antigen is the major capsid protein, not the E6 and E7 oncoproteins.

questions.stem: Routine cervical cytology from a 32-year-old woman shows squamous epithelial cells with enlarged, dark, wrinkled nuclei surrounded by a zone of clear cytoplasm. Infection with which of the following viruses is most likely responsible for these changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Herpes simplex virus type 1

choices.label: B
choices.text: Herpes simplex virus type 2

choices.label: C
choices.text: Human immunodeficiency virus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Human papillomavirus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Varicella zoster virus

explanation.summary: Koilocytes, with large, dark, raisinoid nuclei and a perinuclear halo, are the cytopathic effect of HPV on cervical cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: HPV causes cytopathic effects on cervical epithelial cells called koilocytes. Their nuclei are large, dark, and often wrinkled (raisinoid), and they often have clear cytoplasm around the nucleus (perinuclear halo). These can be seen on a Pap smear.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HSV-1 produces multinucleated giant cells and Cowdry A inclusions, not koilocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HSV-2 produces multinucleated giant cells and Cowdry A inclusions, not koilocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HIV does not produce koilocytic change in cervical epithelium.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Varicella zoster virus produces changes like those of HSV (giant cells, inclusions), not koilocytes.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman comes to the clinic because she has noticed several painless, soft, raised growths around her vaginal introitus and perianal skin. Examination shows multiple verrucous lesions, and the diagnosis is made on appearance alone. Which of the following HPV types most commonly cause these lesions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: HPV-1 and HPV-2

choices.label: B
choices.text: HPV-1 and HPV-4

choices.label: C
choices.text: HPV-2 and HPV-4

choices.label: D
choices.text: HPV-6 and HPV-11

choices.label: E
choices.text: HPV-16 and HPV-18

explanation.summary: Anogenital warts (condyloma acuminatum) are caused mainly by low-risk HPV-6 and HPV-11.
explanation.whyCorrect: HPV-6 and HPV-11 are low-risk strains that cause anogenital warts (condyloma acuminatum), which present as warty lesions in the genital or rectal area and are diagnosed by their appearance on examination.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HPV-1 and HPV-2 are cutaneous wart types.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HPV-1 and HPV-4 cause cutaneous warts such as common, plantar, and flat warts.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HPV-2 and HPV-4 are cutaneous wart types.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HPV-16 and HPV-18 are the highest-risk oncogenic types, associated with cervical cancer rather than warts.

questions.stem: A physician unroofs a vesicle on a patient's buttock, stains a scraping of its base, and examines it under a light microscope. The smear shows multinucleated giant cells whose nuclei contain eosinophilic, glassy inclusions with chromatin pushed to the nuclear edge. Which of the following best explains why this test is no longer used for primary diagnosis of herpes simplex infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It cannot show cytopathic change in early lesions

choices.label: B
choices.text: It detects HPV koilocytes rather than herpes effects

choices.label: C
choices.text: It detects only antibodies from a past infection

choices.label: D
choices.text: It requires about 5 days of growth before reading

choices.label: E
choices.text: Varicella zoster virus produces the same changes

explanation.summary: The Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells and Cowdry A inclusions, but these also occur with varicella zoster virus, so DNA testing has replaced it.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Tzanck test visualizes the two HSV cytopathic effects, multinucleated giant cells and Cowdry A inclusions. Both are also seen in other viral infections such as varicella zoster virus, so the smear cannot establish HSV specifically and has been replaced by modern DNA testing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The smear does show cytopathic change; its problem is lack of specificity, not early-lesion blindness.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Giant cells with Cowdry A inclusions are herpesvirus effects, not HPV koilocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antibody detection describes type-specific serology, not a cytologic smear.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The 5-day growth period describes viral culture, not a stained smear.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman at 39 weeks' gestation with known HSV-2 infection comes to the labor and delivery unit in early labor. Pelvic examination shows several active vesicular lesions on the vulva. Which of the following is the most appropriate management to protect the newborn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cesarean delivery instead of vaginal delivery

choices.label: B
choices.text: Induction of labor for rapid vaginal delivery

choices.label: C
choices.text: Vaginal delivery after maternal serology testing

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vaginal delivery after topical trichloroacetic acid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vaginal delivery with a neonatal Tzanck smear

explanation.summary: Pregnant patients with active genital herpes lesions should deliver by C-section to avoid transmitting HSV to the baby.
explanation.whyCorrect: Genital herpes can pass to the neonate during vaginal delivery, causing eye infection and disseminated disease with neurologic, lung, liver, and kidney involvement. It is recommended that patients with active genital lesions have a C-section instead of a vaginal delivery; antivirals before delivery may also decrease transmission.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Speeding vaginal delivery still exposes the newborn to virus in active lesions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Serology detects past infection and does nothing to prevent exposure during delivery through active lesions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Trichloroacetic acid is a caustic wart treatment, not HSV therapy, and should not be applied to mucosa.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vaginal delivery through active lesions exposes the newborn; an outdated smear does not prevent infection.

questions.stem: A virology laboratory characterizes two DNA viruses isolated from genital lesions. Virus X has a linear double-stranded DNA genome, an envelope, and an icosahedral capsid. Virus Y is non-enveloped and has a circular double-stranded DNA genome. Which of the following statements correctly contrasts the life cycles of these two viruses?

choices.label: A
choices.text: X has animal reservoirs; Y infects only human hosts

choices.label: B
choices.text: X integrates into host DNA; Y persists as a neuronal episome

choices.label: C
choices.text: X is latent in basal epithelial cells; Y in sensory ganglia

choices.label: D
choices.text: X is latent in sensory ganglia; Y in basal epithelial cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: X is non-cytolytic in epithelium; Y lyses epithelial cells

explanation.summary: Herpesviruses (enveloped, linear dsDNA) become latent in sensory ganglia; papillomaviruses (non-enveloped, circular dsDNA) become latent in basal epithelial cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Virus X is a herpesvirus (HSV): it is cytolytic in epithelial cells and establishes latency by infecting sensory neurons and migrating to sensory ganglia, where the genome persists as a nuclear episome. Virus Y is a papillomavirus (HPV), which infects basal epithelial cells, where both low- and high-risk strains can become latent.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Both HSV and HPV are obligate human pathogens with no animal reservoirs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HSV persists as a neuronal episome; it is high-risk HPV that frequently integrates into host DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This reverses the two latency sites.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HSV infection of epithelial cells is cytolytic, producing vesicles; high-risk HPV is often nonproductive.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man comes to the clinic because of a sore on the shaft of his penis that appeared 3 weeks after unprotected intercourse with a new partner. Examination shows a firm, round, 1.5-cm ulcer that is not tender, with mild bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy. Which of the following best describes the organism most likely responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enveloped DNA virus that causes grouped painful vesicles

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gram-negative bacillus cultured from a purulent ulcer base

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gram-negative rod often seen inside cells on Giemsa stain

choices.label: D
choices.text: Obligate intracellular bacterium that targets lymphatic tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tightly coiled spirochete best seen with dark-field microscopy

explanation.summary: A firm, painless chancre with bilateral adenopathy is primary syphilis, caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum.
explanation.whyCorrect: The primary chancre is a firm, round, 1-2 cm, usually painless ulcer at the site of entry, often with mild to moderate bilateral lymphadenopathy. T. pallidum is a tightly coiled spirochete that is too thin for routine light microscopy and extremely difficult to culture, so it is visualized with dark-field microscopy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Herpes simplex virus causes tender ulcers; the lack of pain is what distinguishes a syphilitic chancre from herpetic lesions.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This describes Haemophilus ducreyi (chancroid), whose ulcers are painful with a purulent exudate and tender suppurative nodes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This describes Klebsiella granulomatis (donovanosis), which causes beefy red painless ulcers without lymphadenopathy, not a firm round chancre.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This describes the Chlamydia trachomatis subtypes of lymphogranuloma venereum, marked by small papules and inguinal buboes with a groove sign.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a rash and anal discomfort. Two months ago she had a painless vulvar sore that healed without treatment. Examination shows small reddish brown macules on the trunk, palms, and soles that do not itch, patchy scalp hair loss, and several raised, warty, gray-brown lesions on the perianal mucosa. Which of the following best describes the perianal lesions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Beefy red ulcers from an intracellular rod

choices.label: B
choices.text: Condylomata lata of secondary syphilis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gummas arising from granulomatous inflammation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inguinal buboes of lymphogranuloma venereum

choices.label: E
choices.text: New chancres at secondary inoculation sites

explanation.summary: Raised, warty, gray-brown mucous membrane lesions of the mouth, genitals, or anus in secondary syphilis are condylomata lata.
explanation.whyCorrect: Untreated primary syphilis can progress to secondary syphilis, characterized by a diffuse nonpruritic reddish brown rash that includes the palms and soles, patchy alopecia, and condylomata lata: warty, raised, gray-brown lesions on the mouth, genitals, or anus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Beefy red, highly vascular ulcers are the lesions of donovanosis (Klebsiella granulomatis), not raised warty plaques.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gummas are rubbery granulomas of tertiary syphilis that appear 4-10 years after infection, mainly in liver, bone, and testes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Buboes are tender enlarged inguinal or femoral lymph nodes, not mucosal lesions, and are caused by specific C. trachomatis subtypes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A chancre is the firm painless ulcer of primary syphilis at the entry site; secondary-stage mucosal lesions are raised and warty.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man is evaluated for frequent falls, especially in dark rooms. He walks on a wide base and slaps his feet down. Examination shows absent vibration and position sense in both legs and diminished light touch; strength is normal. He recalls a painless genital sore about 25 years ago that was never treated. Serum nontreponemal and treponemal tests are reactive. Degeneration of which of the following structures best explains his deficits?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anterior horn cells of the spinal cord

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anterolateral spinothalamic tracts

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lateral corticospinal tracts of the cord

choices.label: D
choices.text: Posterior columns of the spinal cord

choices.label: E
choices.text: Purkinje cells of the cerebellar vermis

explanation.summary: Tabes dorsalis, a form of neurosyphilis, is degeneration of the posterior columns causing loss of proprioception, vibration, and touch.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neurosyphilis presents 10-30 years after untreated infection. Tabes dorsalis is degeneration of the posterior (dorsal) columns of the spinal cord, producing loss of proprioception (position sense), vibration, and touch, which leads to a sensory ataxia that worsens without visual input.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anterior horn cell loss causes weakness and atrophy; this patient has normal strength with a purely sensory deficit.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The spinothalamic tracts carry pain and temperature; the lost modalities here (vibration, position) travel in the posterior columns.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Corticospinal tract damage produces upper motor neuron weakness and spasticity, not loss of vibration and position sense.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cerebellar degeneration causes ataxia with preserved proprioception; here the ataxia stems from lost position sense.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is evaluated for exertional dyspnea. Examination shows an early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal border. CT angiography shows aneurysmal dilation limited to the ascending aorta; the abdominal aorta is normal. Serum RPR and FTA-ABS are reactive. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of his aortic disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A gumma eroding directly through the aortic root

choices.label: B
choices.text: Atherosclerotic plaque weakening the infrarenal wall

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cystic medial degeneration from a fibrillin defect

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inflammation of the vasa vasorum of the aortic wall

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spirochete vegetations destroying the valve cusps

explanation.summary: Cardiovascular syphilis causes ascending aortic aneurysms through inflammation of the vasa vasorum, often with aortic insufficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: In cardiovascular syphilis, which presents 10-30 years after infection, inflammation of the vasa vasorum (the penetrating arteries that nourish the aortic wall) leads to aneurysms of the ascending aorta. Patients may present with aortic valve insufficiency and a diastolic murmur, as here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gummas are a separate tertiary form, mainly in liver, bone, and testes; syphilitic aortitis results from vasa vasorum inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Atherosclerosis typically causes abdominal aortic aneurysms; syphilitic aneurysms characteristically involve the ascending aorta.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cystic medial degeneration from a fibrillin defect is a connective tissue mechanism, not the lesion of cardiovascular syphilis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cardiovascular syphilis is not a valvular vegetation process; the insufficiency results from aortic root dilation.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman who is not pregnant undergoes STI screening after learning that a former partner has syphilis. She has no symptoms, and examination is normal. A rapid plasma reagin test is reactive at a titer of 1:8. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to establish the diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A treponemal assay such as the TPPA

choices.label: B
choices.text: Culture of T. pallidum from her serum

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dark-field microscopy of a peripheral blood sample

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gram stain of an endocervical swab

choices.label: E
choices.text: Repeat the rapid plasma reagin in 6 months

explanation.summary: A reactive nontreponemal screen must be confirmed with a treponemal test before syphilis is diagnosed.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nontreponemal tests (RPR, VDRL, TRUST) are cheap and sensitive but not very specific, so they are used for screening. Because false positives occur, the diagnosis requires a positive treponemal test (FTA-ABS, MHA-TP, TPPA, TP-EIA, or CIA) as confirmation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: T. pallidum is extremely difficult to culture, which is why diagnosis relies on serologic testing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dark-field microscopy visualizes spirochetes from lesion material; she has no lesion, and blood is not the specimen used.
whyWrongByChoice.D: T. pallidum is difficult to observe on Gram stain, so this would not confirm the diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Waiting 6 months delays confirmation; a reactive screen should be followed now by a treponemal test.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man has a painless penile ulcer, and both nontreponemal and treponemal tests are reactive. He has no neurologic or ocular symptoms and no drug allergies. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G infusions

choices.label: B
choices.text: One intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin G

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oral azithromycin given as a single dose

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral penicillin V taken for several weeks

choices.label: E
choices.text: Three weekly intramuscular doses of benzathine penicillin G

explanation.summary: Primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis are treated with a single IM injection of 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin G.
explanation.whyCorrect: Penicillin G is the treatment of choice for every stage of syphilis. For primary syphilis, a single intramuscular injection of 2.4 million units of long-acting benzathine penicillin G maintains sustained low penicillin levels sufficient for cure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aqueous crystalline penicillin G is given intravenously for neurosyphilis and ocular syphilis, which this patient lacks.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Azithromycin is used for chancroid, donovanosis, and lymphogranuloma venereum, not as treatment for syphilis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oral penicillin should not be substituted for the recommended regimen because it may not achieve adequate exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Three weekly injections are reserved for late latent, gummatous, or cardiovascular syphilis, or latent disease of uncertain duration.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman comes to the physician because of blurred vision in both eyes over the past 2 weeks. Visual acuity is decreased bilaterally, and funduscopic examination shows retinal inflammation. Serum RPR and TP-EIA are reactive. She has no drug allergies. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Intramuscular benzathine plus oral amoxicillin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G

choices.label: C
choices.text: One intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin G

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral doxycycline taken for several weeks

choices.label: E
choices.text: Three weekly intramuscular benzathine penicillin G doses

explanation.summary: Neurosyphilis and ocular syphilis require intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ocular syphilis is a type of neurosyphilis that damages the retina, nerves, and vessels of the eye. Aqueous crystalline penicillin G is a water-soluble IV formulation that achieves the high serum concentrations needed to penetrate sequestered sites such as the CNS and aqueous humor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Combinations of different penicillin preparations should not be substituted for the recommended regimen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A single benzathine dose gives low sustained levels suitable for early syphilis but not adequate penetration into the eye or CNS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Doxycycline is a second-line agent for selected stages in penicillin-allergic, nonpregnant patients; she has no allergy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Three weekly benzathine doses treat late latent, gummatous, and cardiovascular syphilis, not ocular disease.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman at 14 weeks' gestation has a nonpruritic rash on her palms and soles. Nontreponemal and treponemal tests are reactive. She reports that she developed hives and wheezing after taking amoxicillin as a teenager. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A single oral dose of azithromycin now

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ceftriaxone now, without any trial of penicillin first

choices.label: C
choices.text: No therapy until after delivery of the infant

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral doxycycline as a second-line regimen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Penicillin desensitization, then penicillin therapy

explanation.summary: Pregnant patients with penicillin allergy should be desensitized and treated with penicillin, the only therapy proven to prevent fetal infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Penicillin is the only therapy with established effectiveness for preventing placental transmission and treating fetal infection. Pregnant patients with a true penicillin allergy should therefore undergo desensitization and rechallenge under careful observation; a cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone is the typical alternative only if desensitization fails.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Azithromycin is used for chancroid, donovanosis, and lymphogranuloma venereum, not for syphilis in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ceftriaxone is the fallback if desensitization fails; it should not replace an attempt at penicillin in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: T. pallidum crosses the placenta at any stage of pregnancy, so delaying treatment risks congenital syphilis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Doxycycline is an option only for nonpregnant penicillin-allergic patients; pregnant patients should be desensitized instead.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man receives an intramuscular injection of benzathine penicillin G for secondary syphilis. Six hours later he develops fever, rigors, headache, myalgias, profuse sweating, hypotension, and worsening of his rash. There is no urticaria, wheezing, or angioedema. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An exotoxin secreted by rapidly dividing live spirochetes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deposition of antigen-antibody complexes in vessels

choices.label: C
choices.text: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation to penicillin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mass release of PAMPs from spirochetes killed by therapy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spread of surviving spirochetes into the nervous system

explanation.summary: The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction follows syphilis treatment when dying spirochetes release PAMPs that activate pattern-recognition receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Within 24 hours of starting treatment, 10-35% of patients develop a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction with fever, headache, myalgia, rigors, diaphoresis, hypotension, and worsening rash. It is believed to result from release of antigens and inflammatory substances as large numbers of spirochetes die; these PAMPs, hidden while T. pallidum is alive, activate toll-like and other pattern-recognition receptors en masse.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The reaction occurs as spirochetes are being killed by the antibiotic, not from a toxin made by multiplying organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Immune-complex deposition is not the proposed mechanism; the reaction reflects innate sensing of released spirochetal PAMPs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IgE-mediated allergy would typically produce urticaria, wheezing, or angioedema, which are absent; fever and worsening rash fit JHR.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CNS invasion would not explain an abrupt systemic febrile reaction within hours of the first dose.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought for a school physical. His mother received no prenatal care. Examination shows notched, peg-shaped upper incisors, anterior bowing of both tibiae, a flattened nasal bridge, and linear scars radiating from the corners of his mouth. Which of the following additional findings is most likely in this child?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A painless ulcer at a mucosal site

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aneurysm of the ascending aorta

choices.label: C
choices.text: Persistent infectious nasal discharge

choices.label: D
choices.text: Raised gray-brown perianal lesions

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sensorineural hearing loss

explanation.summary: Late congenital syphilis (>2 years) includes Hutchinson teeth, saber shins, saddle nose, rhagades, interstitial keratitis, and sensorineural hearing loss.
explanation.whyCorrect: Untreated congenital syphilis can progress to late congenital syphilis after age 2, with Hutchinson teeth and mulberry molars, saber shins, saddle nose, rhagades (perioral fissures or scars), interstitial keratitis, and sensorineural hearing loss.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A painless ulcer (chancre) marks primary acquired syphilis at the site of inoculation, not congenital infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ascending aortic aneurysm is a manifestation of acquired tertiary cardiovascular syphilis decades after infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Snuffles, a persistent highly infectious nasal discharge, is a feature of early congenital syphilis (<2 years).
whyWrongByChoice.D: Condylomata lata are raised gray-brown mucosal lesions of secondary syphilis, not a feature of late congenital disease.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man returns from several months of work in the Caribbean with two painful genital ulcers. The ulcers have an erythematous base and are covered with a gray-yellow exudate that bleeds when scraped. There is a tender, fluctuant, pus-filled inguinal lymph node on the right. Tests for syphilis and herpes simplex virus are negative. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chlamydia trachomatis L-serovars

choices.label: B
choices.text: Haemophilus ducreyi

choices.label: C
choices.text: Herpes simplex virus type 2

choices.label: D
choices.text: Klebsiella granulomatis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Treponema pallidum

explanation.summary: Painful genital ulcers with purulent exudate and tender suppurative inguinal nodes, with negative syphilis and HSV tests, indicate chancroid (H. ducreyi).
explanation.whyCorrect: Chancroid is caused by the gram-negative bacillus Haemophilus ducreyi, seen mostly in parts of Africa and the Caribbean. Its ulcers are painful, with an erythematous base and gray or yellow purulent exudate that bleeds when scraped, accompanied by tender suppurative inguinal adenopathy. A probable diagnosis is made when syphilis and HSV tests are negative.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lymphogranuloma venereum causes small self-limiting ulcerating papules with buboes and a groove sign, not painful purulent ulcers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HSV causes tender ulcers but has been excluded by negative testing, and it does not cause suppurative nodes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Klebsiella granulomatis causes painless beefy red ulcers without surrounding lymphadenopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: T. pallidum produces a painless chancre, and syphilis testing here is negative.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man who recently moved from Papua New Guinea has a slowly enlarging lesion on the penis. Examination shows a painless, highly vascular, beefy red ulcer that bleeds on contact; there is no inguinal lymphadenopathy. Syphilis serology is nonreactive, and routine bacterial culture of the ulcer grows no pathogen. Which of the following findings would confirm the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A positive nucleic acid test for H. ducreyi

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chlamydial inclusions in an aspirated lymph node

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dark-staining Donovan bodies on tissue biopsy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reactive nontreponemal and treponemal serology

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spirochetes on dark-field examination of ulcer fluid

explanation.summary: Donovanosis (K. granulomatis) is diagnosed by seeing dark-staining Donovan bodies on biopsy, since the organism is hard to culture.
explanation.whyCorrect: Klebsiella granulomatis, a gram-negative bacillus prevalent in India, New Guinea, the Caribbean, central Australia, and southern Africa, causes painless, slowly progressive, highly vascular beefy red ulcers that bleed easily without lymphadenopathy. It is difficult to culture and often intracellular, so diagnosis requires dark-staining Donovan bodies on biopsy (Wright or Giemsa stain). Azithromycin is the treatment of choice.

whyWrongByChoice.A: H. ducreyi causes painful purulent ulcers with tender suppurative nodes, unlike this painless beefy red ulcer.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymphogranuloma venereum causes inguinal buboes; this patient has no lymphadenopathy to aspirate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Syphilis serology is nonreactive here and would not identify K. granulomatis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dark-field microscopy identifies T. pallidum; syphilis serology is already nonreactive and the lesion is not a chancre.
